title: Trigger Price Meaning: Examples, SL Orders and Limit Price
summary: Learn what trigger price means, how it differs from limit price, buy and sell stop-loss rules, and why an order may be rejected or remain unfilled.
body_markdown:
Trigger price is the price level that activates a stop-loss order when the last traded price reaches or crosses it. It determines when the order becomes eligible for execution, not the price at which your trade is guaranteed to execute.


For example, you buy a stock at ₹100 and place a sell stop-loss with a ₹95 trigger. When the stock trades at ₹95 or below, the stop-loss activates. Its execution then depends on the order type, available buyers and any limit price you set.


## What Is Trigger Price in the Stock Market?


An exchange-held stop-loss waits in the exchange’s **stop-loss book** . It is not available for normal matching until its trigger condition is met.


For a stop-loss limit order, triggering releases a limit order into the regular order book.[NSE’s trading-system explanation](https://www.nseindia.com/static/products-services/equity-derivatives-trading-system) also states that the regular-book timestamp is the time of triggering. Placing the stop-loss earlier does not give it that earlier time priority in the regular book.


This differs from a broker-held condition such as GTT, where the broker submits an order after the condition is met.


If you are unfamiliar with market, limit and stop-loss orders, read our guide to[trading order types](https://algotest.in/blog/trading-orders-explained/) .


## Trigger Price vs Limit Price


The trigger decides **when the stop-loss activates** . The limit decides **the least favourable price you will accept** if it executes.

Purpose

Suppose your sell SL order has a **₹95 trigger and ₹94.90 limit** . After activation, it can sell at ₹94.90 or higher if buyers are available. ₹95 is not a ceiling on the selling price.


If available buyers are only below ₹94.90, the order cannot execute against those bids. Triggering alone does not close your position.


## Buy and Sell Trigger Price Rules


For a stop-loss intended to wait before activation, place a buy trigger above the current last traded price and a sell trigger below it.


Order


Typical purpose


Trigger relative to current LTP


Limit-price rule


Buy SL


Exit a short position or enter above the market


Above LTP


Limit must be at or above trigger


Sell SL


Exit a long position or enter below the market


Below LTP


Limit must be at or below trigger


Do not confuse **your original entry price** with the **current LTP** . Order-entry validation uses the current market context. A trigger already reached or crossed may be rejected by the broker or activate immediately, depending on the system.


### Options example: a stop-loss on a short option


Assume you sold a Nifty call option at a **₹100 premium** , and its premium is currently ₹110. You want a buy stop-loss to activate if the premium rises to ₹130.


-


**Order side:** Buy, to close the short option.


-


**Trigger price:** ₹130.


-


**Limit price:** ₹132.


When that option’s LTP reaches or exceeds ₹130, the buy limit order becomes active. It can execute at ₹132 or lower, subject to available sellers and exchange checks. If sellers are only available above ₹132, it may remain unfilled.


These prices refer to the[option premium](https://algotest.in/blog/black-scholes-option-pricing-model) , not the Nifty index level. The ₹2 gap is an illustration, not a recommended buffer for every contract.


For placing a stop-loss on an existing position, see the[AlgoTest Strategy Builder stop-loss doc](https://docs.algotest.in/clicktrade/strategy-builder/additional-information/stop-loss/) .


## Trigger Price in SL vs SL-M Orders


**SL, or stop-loss limit:** You enter a trigger and a limit price. After activation, the order can execute only at the limit or better. It provides a price boundary but may remain partly or entirely unfilled.


**SL-M, or stop-loss market:** You enter a trigger without a limit price. After activation, the order seeks execution at available market prices. The fill can differ from your trigger, especially during a gap or a fast move. Execution still depends on market conditions and applicable controls.


**SL-M orders are not available for options contracts on NSE** , a restriction the exchange introduced to prevent freak trades. Options traders therefore use SL orders, which brings the unfilled risk back into play. Availability also varies by exchange, segment and broker, so check which order types your platform supports before you rely on one.


A wider SL buffer allows execution across more prices, but also permits a worse fill. It does not turn an SL order into a market order or guarantee execution.


## Why Is Your Trigger Price Rejected, or Your Order Unfilled?


First check the order status. Rejected, trigger pending and open after triggering describe different situations.


Situation


What to check


Trigger is on the wrong side of the current price


Check the buy/sell side and current LTP. Apply the stop-loss direction rules, not GTT rules.


Trigger and limit are reversed


A buy SL needs limit ≥ trigger; a sell SL needs limit ≤ trigger.


Trigger–limit gap exceeds the permitted range


Check the exchange’s allowed difference for that instrument and price level.


Limit price fails a separate exchange check


Read the rejection message for price-band or Limit Price Protection restrictions.


Order triggers but remains open


Check whether matching orders exist at your limit or better and whether enough quantity is available.


SL-M is unavailable


Check exchange, segment and broker restrictions; use a supported order type.


NSE’s validation of the **difference between trigger and limit prices** is separate from **Limit Price Protection (LPP)** , which checks limit prices against an allowed range. Reducing your buffer may address the first rejection without resolving the second.


Setting trigger and limit to the same price is not automatically wrong. The order can fill at that price or better, but a quick move beyond it can leave the order unfilled.


For[AlgoTest-](https://algotest.in/) specific buffer settings and unfilled-order behaviour, read the[Limit/SL-L order FAQs](https://algotest.in/blog/faqs-about-sl-l-orders-algo-trading-software-india/) .


## How Is Trigger Price Different in GTT Orders?


A GTT condition is monitored by the broker. When it is met, the broker submits an order to the exchange. Zerodha’s GTT conditions can remain active for up to 365 days, subject to its terms.


GTT can support directions that differ from an ordinary stop-loss:


-


**Buy on a fall:** A stock is at ₹200; a buy GTT can trigger at ₹190.


-


**Sell at a target:** A stock is at ₹200; a sell GTT can trigger at ₹220.


Therefore, “buy trigger above LTP” and “sell trigger below LTP” are not universal rules for every conditional order.


A GTT does not reserve exchange queue priority while it waits at the broker. Once submitted, its order is subject to exchange matching and validation. A triggered GTT also does not guarantee a completed trade.

## Conclusion


The trigger price activates your stop-loss; the order type and limit price determine what can happen next. Check the buy/sell direction, permitted price range and order status instead of assuming that a triggered order has closed the trade.
